title: Extreme-Scale Ising Machines with Cluster Mean-Field Theory
authors: Xiuqi Zhang, Shuvro Chowdhury, Shaila Niazi, Christian Z. Pratt, Navid Anjum Aadit, Kerem Y. Camsari
abstract: Scaling analog and digital Ising machines to larger problems requires overcoming finite device capacity and the cost of communication between devices. We present cluster mean-field theory (CMFT), a framework that partitions a large interaction graph into clusters sized to fit available hardware. Each cluster performs local updates independently, while interactions across cluster boundaries enter through periodically updated effective biases computed from boundary-spin averages. To reduce the error introduced by fixed cluster boundaries, we introduce dynamic partitioning, which cycles through multiple partitions so that interactions approximated by mean fields at one stage can act through instantaneous spins at another. On three-dimensional spin glasses and planted Pegasus instances, dynamic CMFT exhibits power-law decay of residual energy over sweep budgets. This shows that solution quality continues to improve with computational effort despite the mean-field approximation. An automated graph partitioner combined with a weighted recovery ratio provides a practical heuristic for selecting partition combinations on graphs without natural cut directions. We demonstrate CMFT on four GPUs with approximately four million p-bits, reaching comparable energy densities up to 15 times faster than a single-GPU implementation of the full graph. By coupling locally evolving clusters through programmable effective biases, CMFT provides a route to extreme-scale Ising machines on both analog and digital hardware.
summary: This paper introduces Cluster Mean-Field Theory (CMFT) to simulate massive Ising models that exceed available hardware capacity. By dynamically partitioning the graph and updating local clusters using effective biases, the method achieves significant computational speedups. It demonstrates that this approach provides a viable pathway for building extreme-scale Ising machines for optimization problems.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is scaling Ising machine simulations to large problems by overcoming finite device capacity and communication bottlenecks.
main_result: Dynamic Cluster Mean-Field Theory (CMFT) provides a scalable route to extreme-scale Ising machines, achieving significant speedups (up to 15x) on multi-GPU setups compared to full graph simulations.
method: The authors propose CMFT, which partitions the large interaction graph into smaller, hardware-sized clusters. They enhance this with dynamic partitioning, cycling through multiple partitions to reduce mean-field approximation errors.
model_or_system: The model is an Ising system described by an energy Hamiltonian $E(\mathbf{m}) = -\sum_{i<j} J_{ij}m_i m_j - \sum_i h_i m_i$. The simulations are tested on 3D spin glasses and planted Pegasus instances.
key_observables: Residual energy decay ($ho_E$), energy density, and the weighted recovery ratio ($r$).
important_parameters: The size of the graph (up to four million p-bits), the sweep budget, and the approximation error introduced by the mean-field assumption.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that local updates using effective biases derived from boundary-spin averages are sufficient, and dynamic cycling helps mitigate the error from fixed mean-field approximations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the scaling process (partitioning), compare sampling distributions (static vs. dynamic CMFT vs. Boltzmann), and show the power-law decay of residual energy ($ho_E$) over computational effort.
paper_structure: The paper introduces CMFT to handle large graphs by localizing computation. It details the dynamic partitioning scheme, analyzes its performance on spin glasses and Pegasus graphs by measuring energy decay, and concludes with a demonstration of multi-GPU scaling.
why_interesting: While focused on classical optimization, the techniques for handling large, complex interactions via localized approximations (like CMFT) and the analysis of error decay are highly relevant to simulating quantum many-body systems on limited hardware.

Each cluster runs locally on a probabilistic computer. A classical computer collects boundary samples from the clusters and combines their averages with the cross-cluster couplings to compute effective biases. These biases remain fixed during the next block of local updates.
